item.title: Why are some explanations bad?
item.description:
I like understanding things. Many explanations strike me as insufficient, and I wanted to know what features characterize the explanations that frustrate me. I looked through answers to why questions on Quora, found ones I didn’t like, and tried to find patterns in them. So far, I've come up with the following ways that explanations can go wrong:


Insufficient specificity

Often, when I'm asking a why question, a general answer will not satisfy my confusion or curiosity. It’s common, though, to not answer specifically enough, ranking as my top complaint with explanations I looked at on Quora.

Here are some examples of cases where an explanation lacks contrast:

Question

Insufficient explanation

Problem

Why do people believe in the supernatural?

Because they have confirmation bias

Any belief can be related to confirmation bias. What about supernatural beliefs make it more related to confirmation bias than others?

Why do people scroll social media?

Because they get dopamine from doing that

Any behavior could be explained in these terms. What is special about social media?

Why are plants green?

Because they emit wavelengths in the range of 495–570 nm

All green things emit those wavelengths!

Why do shot-for-shot remakes exist?

Profit (based on this)

Any movie could be made with profit in mind. A more complete answer could be:

Shot-for-shot remakes are especially profitable because they walk the line of peoples’ preferences for familiarity and nostalgia with novelty. Most people wouldn’t watch the exact same movie twice in theaters, but they are more interested in a new movie if it’s something they’re already familiar with. 


Interestingly, not all questions should be answered with the specificity that the question asker is looking for. Here are some examples:

Question

Explanation

Why does Bill have four legs?

Because he’s a cat and cats have four legs.

Why do men commit more murders than women?

Because men commit more violence in general. 

Why does [plant species] have chlorophyll?

Because nearly every plant species has chlorophyll. 

At first, I didn't think these were good explanations because patterns are not causal. Being a cat doesn't cause an animal to have four legs. Still, these explanations add relevant information that can clear things up for the question-asker.

Insufficient acknowledgement of counterexamples

Question

Insufficient explanation

Problem

Why do animals like polar bears have thick fur?

Because they need to keep warm (based on this)

This is an okay answer, but not all arctic animals have thick fur. A better answer could be:

Many arctic animals have layers of thick fur, but others have blubber. While blubber is more energetically expensive, hair can become compressed in water, making it ineffective as insulation.

Why don’t sharks have bones?

“Bones are rigid and fixed in length after a species specific period. Cartilage is flexible and can increase in size as critters like sharks continue to grow throughout their lives.” (from this)

Large bony fish exist, too.

To get more specifity, you can try asking questions like:

  • Why do ___ have ___ rather than some other trait?
  • Why do ___ have ___, but others in the same category don’t have this trait?
  • Why __________? Is there a different mechanism behind this than others in the same category?


Insufficient mechanistic detail

Question

Insufficient explanation

Problem

Why is the flame from a gas stove blue?

Blue flames are produced by excited radicals.

I don’t know anything about how radicals would emit light, so I would still be pretty confused.

Interestingly, the following is sufficient for me when it comes to why some flames are orange, suggesting that analogous situations are important:

Soot particles at really high temperatures, similarly to a hot metal, glow orange.

Why does rain fall as small drops?

Because of air resistance (based on this) 

To me, it’s not intuitive how air resistance would make raindrops smaller. I think this could be solved with a good analogy.

Asking for intuitive examples or analogies may help with this problem.

Not the kind of explanation I wanted

There may be a variety of true answers to a “why” question, but they may not all be what you’re looking for. The question "Why are plants green?" can be answered from a variety of perspectives:

Category

Explanation?

Cause?

Before effect?

Example

Historical

Yes

Yes

Yes

Plants are green because an ancestral cell engulfed a photosynthetic cell, which eventually became the chloroplast.

Evolutionary

Yes

Yes

Yes

Plants are green because chlorophyll-based organisms may have outcompeted retinal-based ones, making a chlorophyll-using organism more likely to become the endosymbiotic ancestor of chloroplasts.

Mechanism

Yes

Maybe

No

Plants are green because they contain chlorophyll, which reflects green wavelengths and absorbs others.

Definition

No

No

-

Plants are green because they are perceived as the color we call green.  

Pattern

No

No

Most plants have some green parts.

Interestingly, while the mechanistic answer is most common for the above question, it's often not mechanisms that we're looking for with why questions (usually, that's "how"). 


Here’s an example of an answer that doesn’t address the kind of answer I’m looking for:

Question

Insufficient explanation

Problem

Why don’t more animals eat wood?

Wood contains lignin, which is difficult to break down.

I want it to address something about an evolutionary tradeoff, like:

Wood contains lignin, which is difficult to break down. There are tradeoffs when it comes to processing lignin: it’s abundant, but it’s physically hard, requires a lot of specialized chemical machinery to break down and use as energy, and the chemical machinery involves highly reactive molecules.


It can help when asking a question to think about what kind of explanation you’re looking for. Here’s some ideas:

Category

Subcategory

Example questions

Historical

Historical origin

What is the historical origin of _____?

Evolutionary

Arbitrary/ random

Why is _____ so common? Was it beneficial or selected for, due to random chance, linked to something that was adaptive, or a spandrel?

What is the evolutionary tradeoff related to ___?

Adaptive/ beneficial

Genetic hitchhiking

Spandrel

Mechanism

Mechanism

What is the mechanism underlying _____  at the [cellular/ atomic/ etc.] level?


Circular or semantic

Next, there are circular and semantic explanations. For "why are plants green?" you could answer "they are the color we call green." I don't think these are super common, and I didn’t find examples of this on Quora.

Question

Insufficient explanation

Why do people look for evidence that confirms their beliefs?

Because they have confirmation bias.


Miscellaneous problems

Question

Insufficient explanation

Problem

Why is Pluto no longer considered a planet?

Because Pluto shares its orbital area with many other objects.

Did the definition change, or did we learn something new about Pluto? If the definition changed, was it for a particular reason? Does the new definition draw a line that reflects reality?

Why are wolves considered evil?

Because we learn to think of them as evil as children through fairytales.

Confuses correlation with causation; why did people make them evil in fairytales?

Why don’t other sharks normally grow as large as great white sharks?

“Short answer is that they are different species.” (from this)

I would want something related to ecological tradeoffs… This doesn’t even provide new information.


Explanations are overrated

While I've focused here on explanations, which are often causal, I think we might spend too much of our limited attention focused on causality. Patterns and descriptions can, and do, help us make decisions.

For instance, imagine you have a symptom that is highly correlated with having a particular disease. If we have a treatment for that disease, it makes sense to test for that disease based on this correlation. Another example: I’ve performed a couple weeks of extensive mood tracking, finding that most evenings and weekends I have pretty high moods, while I have lower moods at work. It made me think that, if I could find things to improve my mood at work, that would have a much larger impact on my overall happiness than trying hobbies I might enjoy more.

Modern science produces lots of experiments and other non-experiments trying to make causal claims. Some have critiqued this movement away from descriptive research (i.e. Grimaldi & Engel 2007). As an example of fascinating and modern descriptive work, Patty Brennan’s career has been centered on animal genitalia, and I would highly recommend this video or this article. 


Understanding things requires a mix of descriptive and causal information. Perhaps my desire to understand focuses too much on the latter, as even this essay is an attempt to see what causes me to not like certain explanations.


Thank you to my friends for providing me with feedback! :)

item.title: Hindsight: a trivia + calibration game
item.description:
I made a betting game called Hindsight (AI slop rulebook at https://hindsight.markets/rules). At last year’s Metagame conference I playtested a face-to-face version but ultimately we gave up trying to come up with methods to trade the chips around conveniently.

The online version is a “TV party game” like JackBox where players view public info on a common screen and private info and decisions on their phones.

Each player starts with 100 chips. The game progresses in a series of rounds until all players but one are bankrupted. In each round there’s a hidden target year between 1900 and 1999. The round has three stages and during each stage:

  1. A clue is revealed about the year—a birth, death, or event (“Grand Rapids, Michigan becomes the first city in the world to add fluoride to its public drinking water”).
  2. There’s an auction in which the players bid down how wide a market they’re willing to make (“I’ll quote a market six years wide”… “I’ll do four”…).
  3. Then the market maker presents a bid and ask price and everyone else must buy or sell N contracts with the market maker where N is the round number. (The escalating stakes prevent the game from going on forever.)

After all three stages, the year is revealed and the contracts settle at one chip per year of distance. The slop rulebook includes other details like who eats the losses when someone goes bankrupt.

item.title: Some interesting internal documents from Anthropic litigation
item.description:
Anthropic released some documents earlier this year due to the book copyright litigation. I think a few of those documents might be of interest to some people here and haven't gotten much attention. In this post I link to some of those documents, and quote the bits I find interesting.[1] (This expands on my quick take from yesterday.)

These aren't Anthropic's official opinions about anything, and you should probably treat opinions in these documents as "what the author thought at the time", not as a corporate stance.

Concise Research Roadmap

It describes Anthropic's research plans in July 2021:[2]

Long Term Goal 

Our top level goal is to work towards the creation of safe, beneficial AGI.

As a proof of concept, we are working to develop a general AI assistant that can interact conversationally with a user to create, edit, and explain software. The most ambitious and successful version of this agent could answer general questions, write functions, identify bugs, design an API, discuss style and best practices, etc -- it would display all the capabilities of a software engineer colleague. We don't expect to reach this goal right away, but it's the direction in which we're striving. 

Our research projects can all be viewed as attempts to understand and construct aspects of this proto-AGI. We currently think this will require large generative models with long memories, fine tuned via RL using both automated rewards and human feedback.

In the pretraining section:

Study the science of:

  • ML advances needed to train arbitrarily large models (1T and larger) while well-optimizing their capabilities for future use and further finetuning
  • Very large contexts (or some equivalent to pack in a great deal of memory/experience)
  • Data quality, including filtering, transfer, finetuning, and diversity, setting the stage for comparisons with RL environments relevant for more advanced models

It predicted the usefulness of RL for tool use pretty early:

RL for Tool Use

Primary goals:

  • Advance our understanding of the path to AGI by exploring the ability of large LMs to use tools and learn about / generate data about their environments and goals
  • See clear signs of life on search, printf debugging, and other valuable tasks, evaluate whether tool use and RL are dissolving the limitations of current large LMs
  • Identify training techniques that produce a more favorable scaling with training compute as compared to supervised learning

Another employee's comments on that document:

I'm a bit nervous if we end up doing alignment research on natural language and capabilities research on code. It feels like there should be a pretty tight connection between the two at all times. If we're not improving capabilities in the domains we're doing alignment research on, it puts limits on how much we can test alignment and how useful the alignment work can be. That could have knock-on effects like alignment becoming an island because we don't integrate it early on.

A possible principle: "by default, capabilities and alignment research should be in proportion across domains unless we can give a good argument for why they should come apart". Is this a good/bad principle?

Data Hypotheses

It describes hypotheses (the author doesn't "believe any of them with very high probability") about what training data is useful. Among other things, it suggests training on Chinese text to slow down Chinese AI labs:

The China Competition Hypothesis – China seems like it might be the least ethical / safe AI actor. To the extent we can slow them down by absorbing market share they could grab (and thereby use to accelerate production of large models), we can tip the geopolitical balance. As a result, we should prioritize having good linguistic performance on languages for markets Chinese companies might be inclined to go after – Mandarin (although Chinese government intervention will likely push us out here), but perhaps also neighbors or countries deeply involved in the Belt and Road strategy.

A comment on the doc:

Some related comments from @ben@anthropic.com --

  • Chinese may still be valuable for all the Chinese diaspora/expats
  • +1 transfer knowledge from Chinese to English
  • Unlikely China will enforce copyright on US?
  • US gov’t may be interested in Chinese language ability for national security reasons, if we end up engaging there

All Company meeting!

This is a June 2021 slideshow[3] that discusses hiring, office space, the efficiency of training trillion parameter models, RL, sources of training data, and interpretability. It discusses Anthropic's first alignment failure in the "RL Update" section:

  • Now running simplest-possible tool-use env
  • Codewhack:
    • Agent gets some words from a Github repo
    • Agent needs to pick a search query that gets exactly one hit.
  • Seemed to work! But,

[next slide]

  • Actually our first alignment failure.
  • Examples:
    • " script that looks at instargram" => "^"
    • " = img.shape[:2]\n\n " => "^"
    • "docker.utils.mkbuildcontext(" => "^"
  • What’s happening?
    • “^” is the regex start of sequence token.
    • There’s only one start of sequence!
    • I didn’t escape the query.
    • I did not end the universe. This time.

Product visions for early 2025 (written in June 2023)

It discusses potential use-cases for Claude 18 months in the future, as of June 2023. At the bottom (in the blue text[4]), various Anthropic employees provide their own takes.

It suggests setting an ambitious goal (transformative AI) and breaking it down into stepping stones that show progress and profit along the way, like SpaceX:

We'll want to find clear stepping stones between where we are now and the long term vision, where we get technological proof points and market feedback along the way. Companies like Magic Leap that aim straight for their super-ambitious final destination end up disconnected from reality and burn an obscene amount of money, ultimately falling behind competitors who were able to absorb market feedback and build organizational muscle. SpaceX is probably a great example of doing this right. The founders (yes, there's more than one!) had the borderline ridiculous goal of achieving human settlement on Mars, but they broke it down into a series of steps that achieved proof points and profit along the way. First they got good at building small, profitable, low cost rockets, then they got good at building medium sized, profitable, low cost rockets, then they figured out how to make rockets reusable to further lower the cost, then they became the world's largest provider of orbital launch capability with their superior product, then they built the world's largest rocket and almost got it into space on the first try… and if they can generate enough demand for heavy lift launch capability, then they can mass produce these giant rockets and start sending them to Mars. The long term goal kept the team inspired and focused, and the steps along the way gave the team the skills and the revenue to succeed.

It discusses "three major visions for TAI": "Claude the Virtual Employee" (also called "Claude the Robot"), "Claude the personal assistant" (also "Claude the Cyborg"), and "Claude as intelligent org infrastructure". It says working on Claude the Virtual Employee and Claude as org infrastructure are useful to "reduce TAI risk", and Claude the personal assistant is "Sort of" useful for reducing TAI risk.

Responsible Scaling as a Framework for Anthropic

It is a slideshow that discusses the RSP and why Anthropic scales capabilities.

Interpretability & Alignment, or Bankruptcy

  • Sometimes folks ask if product is just here to "fund alignment & interpretability research"...
  • But you can also argue for the opposite:
    • In worlds where alignment is extremely difficult or impossible, these teams need to save the world by demonstrating this fact persuasively
    • In worlds where alignment is easy/manageable, these teams need to save the company by making responsible scaling well-defined and achievable

This is a bit of an exaggeration, but not too much. We're all working together to accomplish a common mission.

It has a diagram of Anthropic's business model:


Slack messages

I had Claude make a thingie to read Slack messages from the filings.

  • These are mostly uninteresting.
  • Teal = Claude 3 Opus, Dove/Firefly/Wombat = Claude 3.5/3.6/3.7 Sonnet according to Anthropic's table.[5]

Conclusion

Keep in mind that these documents weren't intended to be public, they aren't Anthropic's official position on anything, and were written in the past. I don't want anyone to get the impression that any of these documents represent commitments from Anthropic to do anything; instead you should think of these as information about what some people at Anthropic were thinking about in the past.

Also keep in mind that this isn't a random sample of documents. The documents Anthropic releases due to litigation are strongly tilted towards being about training data because Anthropic gets sued over their training data a lot, and doesn't get a lot of lawsuits related to things like alignment science. You should also consider that Anthropic might try harder to redact information that makes them look bad. Most of the documents I looked at are things like Data Partnerships <> Finance; Monthly Syncs which is heavily redacted and much less interesting.[6]

Thanks to Anthropic and the authors of these documents for creating them; I enjoyed reading them! Also thanks to the Free Law Project for running RECAP/CourtListener, which is where I got these documents from. (Perhaps I should get a PACER account so I can access documents that aren't already in RECAP.)

I'll probably get back to focusing on technical alignment research now, but reading obscure documents about Anthropic has been a fun hobby!

Anthropic's codename table is pretty weird - e.g. "Santa" is a codename for all Claude models from Claude 1 to Claude 2.1, except Claude Instant 1 and Claude 2. At first I thought it was something like the base model, but that would imply that Claude 2.1 used an older base model than Claude 2?

item.title: PPA 11: The Basic Model
item.description:
[This is the eleventh piece in my series on the Parametric Process Assumption (PPA), a new model of anthropics. You should start here if you are just seeing this for the first time.

The previous piece is "Deriving the PPA."

This piece is part of the technical portion of this series.

TLDR:

  • Most of this piece contains proofs for the statements in this piece
  • We prove the PPA is negligibly presumptuous, in the sense that, when modeling life emergence as a Poisson point process, we have a presumptuousness of exactly one additional species
  • We define anthropic temporally consistency in terms of random processes and show that the PPA, liked the SIA, is temporally consistent

The next piece will be on the using the PPA with infinite universes, and is coming soon.]


At the start of this series, we introduced the “Basic Model” of anthropics. In the Basic Model, the universe is a large random process, and as this process progresses it sometimes spawns subprocesses that generate observers. The parameter of our model, which we call the “propensity for life,” is the average number of times one of these sub-processes emerges.  “Propensity” is a stand-in for the size of everything that exists across any potential multiverse, and it is epistemic - fixed but otherwise unknown, like the digits of pi.

The actual progression of one of these observer-generating processes, once they are kicked off, is random/aleatoric. The typical example of one of these “sub-processes” would be a species that emerges and keeps breeding until it either goes extinct or perhaps colonizes the stars. Other examples might be one-off Boltzmann Brains or large-scale simulations. As is often the case with priors, our criteria for defining an observer-generating process is somewhat subjective, but - with one subtle exception - most choices will give us reasonable results as long as we don’t go out of our way to do anything too pathological.

For instance, it makes little difference if we measure our processes according to “species” or “life-bearing planets,” since both of those things represent well-defined sets of observers with beginnings and ends. But we don’t want to go too small; defining each observer to be its own process (so that propensity = numbers of observers in the universe, i.e. ) would just devolve the PPA into the SSA. The goal really is to select the largest granularity where we feel that the size of the process is primarily determined not by unknown laws of physics, but by randomness within the laws we already have. The speed of light, for example, is probably not relevant to whether our species continues to exist for another 10 years or another 10,000, and neither is the existence of a multiverse for that matter. But the size of the multiverse obviously would matter if we wanted to count the number of species throughout existence.

To be more explicit, our model will comprise three different sets of variables, which you may have already seen in a previous piece:

  • (Epistemic) Propensity for Life: How many times does an observer-creating process emerge, on average?
  • (Aleatoric) Longevity: For each emergence, how many observers does the process produce before it terminates? 
  • Diversity: Everything else. When a process starts, what do the observers experience? What do they look like? etc.

Notation

We will eventually expand the model to include large-scale simulations and Boltzmann Brains as additional types of subprocesses, but for most of this discussion we’re just going to focus on “species” subprocesses, and this notation will focus only on that for now. It should be understood though that “species” is a shorthand for “observer-generating process that works approximately like what we see on Earth.” If you want to expand it to, say, all life on the planet, then that doesn’t change the model even if the word “species” becomes less applicable.

We’ll represent the epistemic propensity parameter as , which for the time being will be a single non-negative number telling us the average number of species. Propensity is only an average, but the actual number of species produced by a given aleatoric universe will be represented by the random variable , where . 

A universe produces exactly species , each having a “longevity” of observers. This means that (ignoring simulations and Boltzmann brains) the total number of observers in any given universe is . We will often use as a shorthand to indicate whichever species we currently belong to. The expected longevity over all species in all possible universes is a known constant . For now we will assume is finite but will discuss the infinite case in the next piece.

Diversity we will also consider aleatoric, and we will represent it with the random variable . We're going to play this variable a little fast and loose because it's not actually that important. For simplicity, we're going to only deal with the species level diversity, meaning each species gets it's own draw (hence the subscript in ). For instance, perhaps would indicate that we have two arms, two legs, and exist on a planet like Earth. The specifics matter very little. In fact, does not need to be only aleatoric - the laws of mathematics and physics are likely responsible for our distribution over , and we could in theory treat our prior over this distribution as an epistemic parameter. As we will prove (and as we saw before), this won’t affect our model. The same irrelevance result would also apply to any randomness an observer observers that doesn't directly give them evidence about propensity or longevity.

An observer is uniquely identified within a universe as - the th member of the th species. We’ll use to indicate the set of observers within species . We won't worry about anything an observer learns not related to information about propensity or longevity.

Poisson Universe

One assumption we will use going forward is that (in the species-only model) is a rate parameter to a Poisson Point Process. For those of you unfamiliar, a Poisson Process is a random process where, with some constant rate, we assume that at any moment/location a particular event can happen. Specifically, we assume that there is some event that happens at any time with a given rate, such that this event can happen independently at any time. This is basically the simplest form of assuming that life is distributed uniformly throughout our universe/multiverse - in expectation it can happen anywhere.[1]

Life emergence is obviously not equally likely once you condition on a particular patch of spacetime looking a particular way, but the approximation is justified because there is no universal canonical coordinate system to the universe, meaning a priori no particular “region” is more likely than another to contain life. This doesn’t quite hold temporally, since there is a universal notion of order to time, but it does work across spatial dimensions and sub-universes in a multiverse, so we’re going to use this approximation anyway. Future work can explore alternatives, but I suspect they will contain no interesting insights.

The Predictions

In the intro to this series, we listed all of the main failure modes of existing anthropic models, claiming that the PPA did not suffer from these failures. Our plan is to go through these one at a time, proving each one under the Basic Model not just for the PPA, but also for the SSA and SIA. 

Independence Results

Before we dig in, though, we have to establish a couple independence results. Using an indexical distribution replaces our prior with a completely different distribution, so it’s important to understand how the relationships between these variables are affected when we go indexical:

  1. Under the SSA, SIA, and PPA, diversity updates independently of both propensity and longevity 
  2. Under the SIA and PPA, longevity updates independently of propensity
  3. Under the SSA, propensity and longevity are positively correlated when you learn indexical information about either one. In the limit of high propensity, this effect disappears and longevity updates do not affect propensity.

An important complexity here is that when we say “diversity” or “longevity” (but not propensity!) we are making indexical statements - we are referencing the values these variables take within our own species, whichever one that may be. Under the SSA, for instance, learning that propensity is low will also cause you to specifically update towards your own species having low longevity.

The SIA is fully presumptuous and the PPA is negligibly so 

By presumptuousness, I mean that it forces us to assume there are an arbitrarily large number of other species in the universe besides ourselves. Although we already discussed this at length in an earlier piece, the Basic Model gives us a way to formally show our work.

As we mentioned, all three variable types in the Basic Model were independent under the SIA and PPA. The most important offshoot of this is that the distribution of species looks the same wherever it emerges. 

One thing I naively believed at one point was that the SIA’s largeness bias only applied to exact clones of yourself, or at least only to observers whose experiences are indistinguishable from your own. The idea was that if you had some subset of observers who all had the same experience, then - in other words, every universe is re-weighted according to the number of clones of that observer it contains.

Therefore, the SIA forces you to re-weight by the number of possible locations, and presumptuousness applies not just to clones, but to our entire understanding of the universe.

[This is the tenth piece in my series on the Parametric Process Assumption (PPA), a new model of anthropics. You should start here if you are just seeing this for the first time.

The previous piece is "Putting it All Together."

This piece starts the more technical portion of this series.

TLDR:

  • We make formal the repetition argument from the intro this series, showing that repeated sampling of the universe specified by some parameter creates an SIA instance nested inside an SSA instance.
  • The argument from repetition cannot eliminate parameters that often lead to empty universes, so we add an "existential term" and call the result the PPA.

The next piece is "The Basic Model."]


The Argument from Repetition

In a previous piece, we discussed how repeating species draws under the SSA causes it to converge to something a bit like the SIA.

Here we’re going to formalize that. We’ll start with some universe prior  over universes , and then make that indexical by adding in another set of observer assignment variables , such that assigning to value corresponds to the logical predicate “I am observer ” We then define a joint distribution over and . Each universe is also associated with a set of observers, corresponding to the observers who actually exist in that universe.

The two most common indexical distributions are:

  • The SSA:  if , and 0 otherwise

where is the number of observers in universe .

To represent what happens when universes are redrawn, we will add an additional parameter , from which we can draw universes . Our universe prior will be extended into a joint distribution over both and . We will sometimes refer to as “epistemic” and as “aleatoric” or the “process variable.”

Then we can define the “argument from repetition”: 

Argument from Repetition (AFR): Define to be the indexical distribution formed from the following sampling procedure:

  • Sample from  
  • Sample aleatoric universes from
  • Select uniformly from the disjoint union

This is just describing the basic procedure we previously used when talking about parametric models and large-universe SSA: for each possible value of , imagine arbitrarily many samples, put all the observers from these samples in a pile, and then select one at random. If we applied this to the Sleeping Beauty problem, for instance, we would flip a bunch of coins and get a sequence (say, H H T) and then select uniformly from an associated set of universe-observer pairs (e.g. , just as we did in the intro to this series. (In the Sleeping Beauty problem, is trivially a singleton since we don't have any epistemic unknowns in the problem setup).

Since for a fixed each universe is sampled in proportion to its likelihood but takes up space in proportion to its size, we have that, in the limit,

Existential Consistency

The one problem with the AFR approach is that it doesn’t do well for which have a high chance of producing no observers. Fortunately, from a model-design perspective, this problem is easy to fix. 

Consider the following situation, which we’ll call God’s Calculation:

To decide if he will create life in the universe, God computes the googolth digit of pi. If it is even, then he creates Adam and Eve. If it is odd, he flips ten trillion coins, and if every single one comes up tails, he creates Adam and Eve. If a single one comes up heads, he creates nothing.

You wake up and discover you are Adam.


Both the SSA and SIA agree in this situation: you should assume that the googolth digit of pi is probably even. But AFR does not: it confidently declares that the digit has . 

The problem is that because we assume the aleatoric parts of the process repeat endlessly, it doesn’t really matter how many flips it takes for God to create life; we have to assume he eventually would.

I don’t have a prefect philosophical answer for this, but I’m leaving that for future work.  For now, though, the problem is very easy to fix mathematically. What we can do is add an adjustment factor that scales each SIA instance by the likelihood that any observers would even exist in that universe, multiplying the probability of each parameter by . This effectively separates each epistemic region of our probability space into a “life exists” and “life doesn’t exist,” then eliminates the “life doesn’t exist” portion.

The implications of this are mostly related to fine-tuning - thanks to this adjustment, the PPA can reproduce the arguments we discussed here.

  • Epistemic: - What are the laws of physics?
  • Existential: - How likely is life to exist under these laws of physics?

item.title: PPA 9: Putting it All Together
item.description:
[This is the ninth piece in my series on the Parametric Process Assumption (PPA), a new model of anthropics.

You should start here if you only want to read one piece on the PPA, but if you only want to read two pieces, this is the second one to read.

The previous piece is "The Fermi Paradox, Fine-Tuning, and the SSA."

TLDR:

  • The SSA's bias for Doomsday only applies if your reference class only includes your own species. The more more species in your universe/reference class, the less Doomsday effect you see
  • The Basic Model of anthropics models the universe as a process progressing randomly until certain relevant subprocesses emerge spontaneously. An intelligent species like humans would be an example of one such process. It has 3 components:
    • (Epistemic) Propensity for Life: How many times does an observer-creating process emerge, on average?
    • (Aleatoric) Longevity: For each emergence, how many observers does the process produce before it terminates? 
    • Diversity: Everything else. When a process starts, what do the observers experience? What do they look like? etc.
  • The previous arguments in this series tell us many things about the Basic Model
    • Diversity has no effect on the SSA, SIA or PPA
    • The SIA acts as an improper prior over longevity but not propensity
    • The SIA gives an undue bias towards large propensity
  • The PPA treats propensity as an epistemic parameter and longevity as aleatoric, avoiding both Doomsday and presumptuousness

The next piece, "Deriving the PPA," begins the more technical portion of this series.]


SSA biases only affect small universes

One frustration for me when I started thinking harder about anthropic philosophy was the slow discovery that many of the worst conclusions of various anthropic models, at least as I understood them, were actually greatly exaggerated. Not all of them, of course, but there were quite a few cases where things treated like foregone conclusions (like the SSA implying Doomsday) often disappeared with certain choices of prior. 

As I've references in this series before, I believe a lot of this comes from the unfortunate tendency to discuss anthropics in terms of small thought experiments, almost always forcing us to choose between exactly one of two universes. This by itself is not a problem - I employed the same tools in several parts of this series - but it runs the real risk of oversimplifying past the point where we are actually saying something applicable.  

Consider, for instance, the Doomsday Argument. Typically, this is presented as a choice between some large universe and some small universe , each with a 50% chance a priori. Every observer, through their birth order, is assigned some number (like your brith rank) and, upon learning your own number, the SSA has you update towards a universe that is more likely in proportion to the ratio between and . For instance, if is 10 and is 20, then finding out we are individual 4 means we are twice as likely to exist in universe :

(If you're coming here straight from the intro, you may wish to take a quick peak at this earlier piece on mosaic plots.)

This is famously countered by the SIA, where L starts out twice as likely and therefore produces no bias when you learn your rank:

The problem with this entire setup, though, is that it assumes our current species is the only one that exists. 

Suppose instead that there were two species within our universe (and our reference class) - one blue and one red - and each was independently assigned to be either “long” or “short”. Our distribution under the SSA would look like this:

Now look what happens when you learn you are the 4th member of the blue species:

The ratio of short to long has evened out considerably from 2:1 to about 1.43:1. Add in an orange species, and the ratio becomes even closer to even at about 1.27:1:

In the limit, as you expand your universe and/or reference class to include more individuals, the shortness bias disappears.

This effect, by the way, does not rely on learning your color in the previous example. Simply knowing that there were more species in consideration is enough to asymptotically eliminate Doomsday bias from the SSA. By the time you get to the kinds of scales that seem likely by our current understanding of physics (see this previous piece), the SSA’s main problematic features - Doomsday and temporal inconsistency - begin to asymptotically vanish.[1] 

The Basic Model

Let’s re-introduce some terminology before we continue. As in the series intro, we’ll call the length of your species - whether it is “long” or “short” - its “longevity,” and we’ll use terms like “shortness bias” to refer to biases in longevity. When we talk about the “size” of the universe, using terms like “largeness bias,” we will instead be talking about the number of species that emerge. 

The previous section showed us that as our lower bound for the size of universe increases, the SSA’s shortness bias decreases with it. The SIA, once you learn your rank in the species, has neither a shortness nor longness bias, but it does have a largeness bias - however big your evidence suggests the universe must be, the SIA insists it must be much much large. In particular, if “infinitely large universe” has even the tiniest bit of positive probability in your prior, then you must discount all other possibilities.

Back when we introduced these terms int he intro, we talked about putting both of them into a single model, which we called the “Basic Model” of anthropics. 

The idea was to imagine the universe as a giant random process, with each independently-emerging species as a subprocess. The exact number of subprocesses (the actual size of the universe) would also be random, but the expected number of subprocesses - the general tendency of the universe to independently create life - would not be random, but rather an epistemic unknown which we called the universe’s “propensity for life.” We illustrated with a toy thought experiment involving a grid of unknown size and spontaneously emerging chains of blue pixels.

The the subprocesses themselves are modeled as completely random, since by the time you get to the granularity of determining a species’ longevity, what you are measuring isn’t really the product of unknown physical laws, so much as randomness within the laws that are already there. The specifics of quantum mechanics or the speed of light, for instance, may have affected the likelihood of humans existing, but probably don’t play largely into how long humanity lasts once it’s here.[2]

Then, we throw in an extra variable to cover all the other facts about our species not related to longevity or propensity, and we get a model with three independent components:

  • (Epistemic) Propensity for Life: How many times does an observer-creating process emerge, on average?
  • (Aleatoric) Longevity: For each emergence, how many observers does the process produce before it terminates? 
  • Diversity[3]: Everything else. When a process starts, what do the observers experience? What do they look like? etc.

Some Observations

There are a few things you should know about the Basic Model and how it behaves under the SSA and SIA. These are things we cover in more detail in the technical portions of this series that follow.

The first is that, as we previously discussed, the diversity term is basically only there to be thrown out. So long as diversity has no a priori effect on longevity (which, in our simplified model, it doesn’t), neither the SSA nor the SIA induce any additional diversity bias one way or the other. It can be safely ignored.

The second is that the SIA cannot really handle infinite propensity - having it as a hypothesis either forces you to insist the universe is infinitely large, or, more likely, just gives you an invalid distribution; this is part of the presumptuous philosopher effect. In the case of infinite longevity, however, the SIA can function as an improper prior, starting essentially undefined but snapping into a proper distribution as soon as we gather some (possibly incomplete) evidence about our rank in our species.

The reason an improper prior only helps with longevity but not propensity is that, at least at the moment, we have no way to learn the propensity of the entire multiverse, which means that we can never update out of the improper regime into something that actually lets us make predictions. Nor, as we discussed, could we ever expect to make such an update. With longevity, we have a well-defined concept like birth rank which can be defined a priori for all observers before our universe is actually sampled; to get an equivalent metric for species index, you would need to acquire some sort of global information about all species in the universe like "ranked distance to largest star" or even just "Nth species ever created," and even that would not localize you within the multiverse.

As for the SSA, we already mentioned that large propensity means that it loses its shortness bias, and in the limit of infinite propensity the SSA’s longevity distribution looks exactly like the SIA’s. But the SSA only handles longevity well if you already have reason to believe your universe's minimum propensity is high. While I did argue that high minimum propensity is probably accurate, if you don’t agree, then under the Basic Model the SSA will have both a smallness bias and a shortness bias. The SIA’s biases are not correlated in this fashion, so learning your rank only eliminates longevity biases without touching the largeness. 

Neither approach, therefore, can simultaneously handle all longevity and propensity values to our satisfaction. But the previous results do suggest a way forward: what we need is a distribution that treats longevity just like the SIA/infinite-propensity SSA, but doesn’t unduly bias us towards one propensity or the other. 

Which, you presumably already know, the PPA does handle both approaches.

The PPA, In Summary

Since introducing the PPA way back in the series intro, we haven’t actually spoken about it much. If you recall, the PPA operated by dividing the variables in our universe into two components: an aleatoric “process” portion and an epistemic “parameter” portion. In later pieces, we connected this to the concept of “parametric models” in Bayesian statistics.

The motivation for this dichotomy was the “argument from repetition,” where we showed that if you took, say, the Sleeping Beauty problem and sampled it over and over again, then whether you wound up deriving the SIA or the SSA depended, respectively, on whether your probability was aleatoric or epistemic. To create an epistemic unknown, we imagined the scientists in the Sleeping Beauty problem calculating the googolth digit of pi instead of using a coin. This was a value that would never change over repetitions, but was nonetheless unknown to us.

The PPA, we said, was just what happens when you applied this reasoning to a more complex universe model. The Basic Model is that more complex model, where we treat propensity like the digits of pi and longevity like a coin flip. The universe (or multiverse) gets sampled, in a virtual sense, over and over again, such that all possible species longevities occur at precisely the expected prior rate; longevity predictions converge the same way they did in large-universe SSA. As for propensity, even though the actual number of species in each of these resamples varies, the average across all of them stays fixed. So propensity remains SSAish, even as longevity becomes SIAish.[4]

And that’s about it, at least until we get more technical in the next couple pieces. There’s an extra term I’ll discuss there to correct for very low-propensity universes, and we'll need to do some work with limits to make the infinite cases work how we want them to. Aside from that, though, we've covered most of the key ideas. You can think of the PPA, as I originally did, as nesting the SIA inside the SSA, or you can simply think of it as just taking the SSA to infinite propensity and then backfilling that structure to finite propensity. I think both approaches take you to the same place.

The next piece, "Deriving the PPA," begins the more technical portion of this series.

  1. ^

    There is an important requirement here, which is that you must assume all species longevities are drawn from the same distribution. Or, to be precise, that they are drawn from distributions with the same mean.

  2. ^

    That said, one might still wonder if it makes more sense to think of the average longevity of all species as a parameter fixed by the laws of physics. I will discuss this in a piece I plan to publish within the coming weeks. This can be added to the model, and it does have a Doomsdayish effect, but I also believe there are good reasons not to make any part of longevity a parameter.

  3. ^

    Diversity has no epistemic/aleatoric label because it does not effect our model which one you assign it

  4. ^

    The PPA actually does have a real but almost negligible presumptuousness from two effects:

    1. The existential term: The PPA's down-weighting of universes where observers are unlikely to exist (as in the previous piece) causes a small asymptotically disappearing pull towards larger universes
    2. Since randomness within the universe is handled in an SIAish way, there is a tiny increase in presumptuous round this. In the model we'll use in the next sections, this will add exactly 1 additional species.

item.title: PPA 8: The Fermi Paradox, Fine-Tuning, and the SSA
item.description:
[This is the eighth piece in my series on the Parametric Process Assumption (PPA), a new model of anthropics. You should start here if you are just seeing this for the first time.

The previous piece is "Temporal Consistency and Texas Sharpshooting."

TLDR:

  • The Fermi Paradox is easily resolved by realizing the universe is gigantic. This means that there are a huge number of possible worlds where life is very very far apart, despite the fact that it also abundant throughout the universe.
  • If all you know is that you exist and that the universe is big and random, then the SSA, contrary to popular belief, is sufficient to conclude that life in the universe is abundant. The SIA, on the other hand, adds an additional bias on top.

The next piece is "Putting it all Together."]


Big and Sparse

I confess that I’ve never really understood the Fermi Paradox. Or at least, I never understood why everyone always seemed so surprised by it.

If you haven’t heard, the Fermi Paradox is the apparent contradiction that, due to the vast age of the universe and the (seemingly) high probability of alien life, we should be observing signs of intelligent alien life all around the universe, and yet we don’t. If near-lightspeed travel were possible, for instance, it would presumably only take an intelligent species a few million years to colonize the entire Milky Way. For a galaxy that’s been around more than 13 billion years, the argument goes, you’d think someone would have gotten to that by now, right?

I do personally believe our existence implies other life is likely to exist somewhere, but the problem with the Fermi Paradox is that it’s not just assuming that life is likely to exist, but that life is likely to be dense. Maybe an intelligent species could theoretically populate the entire Milky Way in a few million years, but why do we expect there to be more than one intelligent species in a given galaxy? Why do we expect there to be more than one intelligent species in the closest thousand galaxies?

I’m not the first to make this point, and I won’t be the last, but if we’re going to attempt a coherent theory of anthropics, the point needs to be made here: the universe, it turns out, is really really big. 

The observable universe - just the observable part, which may or may not make up only an infinitesimal percentage - has a radius of 46.5 billion light-years, literally millions of times more than the range at which we can supposedly find life.[1]

Lower estimates tell us the number of galaxies in the observable universe measures a few hundred billion; let’s say for the sake of argument that the number is 200 billion. This means that the chance of intelligent life existing in any particular galaxy could be 1 in a million, and there would still be 200 thousand different planets out there just teeming with intelligent life, each one hundreds of millions of light-years away from its closest life-bearing neighbor. 

I know this is the “low math” track of this series, but I cannot resist the temptation to drive this point with just a tiny bit of math. Let’s label the physical extent of the universe X, where X is basically any measure of size, such as "number of galaxies" in our last example. Then let’s declare another variable Y, which we’ll call the “life density” of the universe. Y tells us, for one unit of size, how many times we expect life to emerge in that region. So if the universe is 100 universe units, and Y is 1/10, then on average we would expect to see life spontaneously emerge in the universe 10 times - X times Y. This value, X times Y, is what we’ll call the universe’s “life propensity.”

We can guess at lower bounds for X, but we don’t know Y at all. In the example above, X was “number of galaxies”, and I suggested the density Y could be maybe 1/1,000,000. But it could reasonably be orders of magnitude lower than that. If the actual density was 1 in a billion, there would still be, in expectation, 200 intelligent species within the observable universe; the chance of life existing somewhere, anywhere, would still be effectively 100%. 

This point is very hard to overstate: if X is large, the range of possible values for Y is massive. If we selected a value for Y “at random,”[2] then we could wind up with virtually anything. To get a feel for it, even if we were to assume that literally nothing existed (or even could exist) outside of the observable universe, then the range of possible densities would look something like this gigantic thing:

Near the lower half of this range, even traveling many times the speed of light would not get aliens in range of humanity, even if they somehow knew which direction to go in.

And, I must remind you, this is assuming the observable universe is literally the only thing that exists. If anything exists outside the observable universe, and especially if there’s a multiverse, then the red part of this chart would go on basically forever. If you could go many times the speed of light, and even if you know which direction to go in, you might never reach another civilizaiton.

Just ask the SSA 

Nothing above is really all that new. These ideas are related to things like the Anthropic Principle, and they come up all the time, not just when talking about the Fermi paradox but also in discussions about cosmic fine-tuning. Across all kinds of contexts, the question “why do we exist at all” is very easily answered by “because the universe is big enough and random enough that life has a high chance of emerging at least somewhere.”

Now, I never know how much to claim “most people” believe something, but at least in many cases I’ve seen, the default assumption seems to be that if you want to believe in a big universe, then you really ought to adopt the SIA. But that’s not actually true. In fact, I would (and will) argue that the conclusions I drew above are actually more aligned with the SSA.

I think the disconnect comes from the fact that when people talk about the SSA or SIA, they typically focus on universes where at least one observer always exists. Sleeping Beauty must choose between one version of herself or two, the presumptuous philosopher must select between a trillion humans or a trillion trillion. For possible universes where no one might exist, however, the SSA and SIA basically take the same attitude, which is to say “that universe isn’t possible.” If there was a 20% chance Sleeping Beauty wouldn’t wake up at all, both the SSA and SIA would give that possibility 0% probability. The SSA’s famous smallness bias does not extend to the situations where nothing actually exists.

Let’s go back to playing dice. Suppose your friend Jim rolls some number of ten-sided dice, say N dice. You don’t know N, but after he’s finished rolling, he comes to you and tells you whether any of the dice came up 10. Not which die, not how many dice there were, just “yes, at least one of them was 10,” or “no, none of them were 10s.”

If getting a 10 corresponds to the observation that life exists, then 1/10 is the life density (because of the ten-sided die)[3], and N is the size of the universe. The propensity is the expected number of times he gets a ten, and that’s N/10. Since we don’t know which roll got the 10, this is equivalent to us knowing we exist, but not our relation to other species which may also exist.

What we want to know is, once we learn that Jim has rolled at least one 10, what credence should we give to each possible value of N? As with all anthropic problems, we’d have to start with a prior over universes (like the 50% chance of heads or tails in the Sleeping Beauty problem) and then see how our anthropic assumptions distort that prior. For the sake of argument, let’s say that N can be, with equal likelihood, any value between 0 and 100:


Now, having learned that Jim has rolled a 10, let’s go through each possible value of N and update our predictions accordingly by removing the percentage of rolls which would not get 10. The first thing we do is eliminate N = 0  - no dice means no chance of rolling 10. N = 1 reduces by exactly 90%, to 1/10 of its original value, since that’s the chance of a single die succeeding. With a little calculation, we find that N = 2 is reduced by 81% of its original value, to just under 20% of where it started. At N = 10, we’re down by about 35% of our original value, and by the time we reach N = 100, while rolling a 10 still isn’t technically guaranteed, our original prior is only adjusted by 0.003%. For all intents and purposes, if you roll a hundred 10-sided dice, you can be pretty damn sure you’ll get at least one 10. Hell, even if you roll only 50 10-sided dice, you can still be pretty sure at least one will come up 10.

However, since this process didn’t actually tell you which die came up 10 (by anaolgy, which observer you are), the SSA makes no further adjustments beyond removing these impossible universes. The SSA therefore transforms the above distribution of universes into something that looks like this:

The result is that universes with low N are more or less eliminated, but high N universes - universes where the size outstrips the density by even a small margin - are left basically unaffected. The flip side of this is that if you believe and/or observe that the density of life is low (e.g. that the dice are many-sided), you must conclude that N is high.[4]

And remember that this is the SSA, the assumption that presumably forces us to be deeply solipsistic. Even there, low density means the universe must be vast. This happens by default, simply because of the SSA’s distortions to the prior.

What about the SIA? In my opinion, it fares worse. The conventional narrative is that the SIA, by virtue of predicting larger universes, is the one that champions hugeness, and that our observations of the universe’s hugeness therefore confirm its accuracy. But what’s actually happening is that the SSA is the one which supports conventional hugeness arguments, and the SIA just throws in some weird, extra bias on top. Specifically, the SIA multiplies the likelihood of each N by about N, creating a completely unjustified assumption that N must be, a priori, quite high:

Ignore anthropics for a second and focus solely on Jim’s dice rolls: how, exactly, are we supposed to motivate a distribution of this shape in that problem? All we know is that there was at least one roll that came up 10. Past maybe 40 rolls, this event is pretty much guaranteed no matter how far above 40 you go. We must, in that situation at least, favor the SSA.

The next piece is "Putting it all Together"

item.title: PPA 7: Temporal Consistency and Texas Sharpshooting
item.description:
[This is the seventh piece in my series on the Parametric Process Assumption (PPA), a new model of anthropics. You should start here if you are just seeing this for the first time.

The previous piece is "Indexical Models Don't Have Diversity Biases."

TLDR:

  • SSA is not "temporally consistent" - learning your brith rank causes an indexical update which can, for instance, change the probabilities of a fair coin that has not yet been tossed
  • In order to perform an indexical update - the kind which causes distortions in the SSA and removes presumptuousness from the SIA - you need to learn your rank relative to some absolute property defined for all observers.
    • Simply using a metric like "closest to the sun" would not help because all observers using such a procedure (picking the nearest star) would always find themselves the closest
    • An actual update would require something like "ranked distance from largest star in the universe" or "life-bearing universe in multiverse with Nth largest gravitational constant," information we could not possibly hope to acquire

The next piece is "The Fermi Paradox, Fine-Tuning, and the SSA."]


One well-established failure mode of the SSA is that it is not "temporally consistent." I believe Nick Bostrom first pointed this out and Joe Carlsmith has an excellent write up on it here. 

The simplest example of inconsistency in the SSA is the Late-Flip version of the Sleeping Beauty Problem where the coin is flipped only after Sleeping Beauty is woken on Monday. In this scenario, P(Heads | Monday) seems as if it must be 0.5, since the coin hasn’t even been flipped yet. The SSA, however, assigns 2/3 credence to P(Heads | Monday).

In that sense, what we mean when we say “temporal consistency” is that for some event X with fixed and known probability, like the flip of a known-fair coin, learning our identity should not alter our credence in X if our identity was set before X happened. But there are two catches to this:

  1. This only applies if the future event has fixed and known probability. If you don’t know whether or not the coin is fair, but then learn that it is 75% biased towards heads, then this will change your credence in the coin going heads even though the event has not happened yet.
  2. When learning something about your identity, there is nothing inherently paradoxical about indexical information changing the credences of past events.

Point 1, I hope, is non-controversial. Point 2 is a bit thornier, and I wouldn’t blame you for arguing we don’t want indexical updates to change the past either. Indeed, in order for temporal consistency to hold in all cases, the only credences it would actually be permissible to distort (as in, alter beyond a normal update on the universe prior) are those on events from before the very first observer was created. 

And it's also true that, upon learning your full identity, the SIA induces no distortions on either the past or the future, so point 2 is unnecessary in that case.

The situation for the PPA is not much worse, though. The PPA still does not distort any events on the same timeline as the universe you are in; the only thing it actually distorts are the credences you give to the parameters of your model, since those are the only things that behave SSAishly. The idea behind parameters however is that they represent fixed laws of math and physics, so - if they can be said to be temporal at all - they are unambiguously “sampled” before the universe or any observers existed. If you buy even the weakest form of point 2, then there is nothing inherently paradoxical about this.

In fact, the way we're using parameters in the PPA (as the variable for expected count of intelligent species) means that it is virtually impossible for us to make an update that causes an anthropic distortion. It would not be enough simply to learn the size of the universe, or that other forms of life existed on other planets. You would have to specifically learn what we're going to call a "nonindexical label" related to your specific place in the universe, which, as we're about to see, can only be done if you already have significant global knowledge of the entire universe's state.

Nonindexical Labeling

Let’s take a step back and talk about what it takes to even trigger the kind of indexical updates that make this sort of discussion necessary. As we saw in the piece on diversity, there is a lot of information about ourselves or the universe for which our credences are unperturbed by the use of indexicals.

Similarly, not every piece of information we learn about ourself will trigger a significant indexical update. To take a simple example, suppose we are in a Sleeping Beauty-like scenario where we are woken up either one day, two, three or four days in a row, starting on Monday. Learning that it was, say, Tuesday, would indeed cause a large indexical update, but merely learning that there had been one other wake-up would only cause an update in the universe prior.


We can see that the first update is indexical because some of the rows are narrowed, whereas the second update is only on the prior because rows are removed but not narrowed. We can also have much smaller indexical updates by only learning, for instance, that there was a wake-up the day before, which instead of narrowing each row to a single observer, merely removes one from each row:

In order to get strong indexical effects it’s not enough to place yourself relative to others; you need to learn your absolute position relative to other observers. This is easy enough to do (in an approximate sense) in the temporal case where your species/experiment has a start time and a well-defined notion of order, but in many cases learning absolute information is almost impossible. In particular, when we’re wondering about things like “how many other intelligent species exist in the universe?” it will be almost impossible to gather information which allows you to do meaningful updates.

Take another look at the 4 wake-up problem from a moment ago, but now imagine that each of these represents a possible intelligent species somewhere in the universe you might have been born into. If you learned you were only species #2, for instance, that would induce the same updates we had upon learning it was Tuesday in the last scenario. Everything would look the same.The question is how we would actually learn we were species #2.

The answer is that we would need some sort of “species rank.” One way to do this would be to do the same thing we did with birth rank, and just order temporally by species emergence in the universe. But how would we ever learn that information? In order to have any confidence that we were actually, say, the 2nd species in the universe, we would first have to map out the entire universe, identify every species in it, and then study their history until we were sure they emerged at a certain time. Only then would we get something like an indexical update.

Except that would only apply for our universe. What if we were in a multiverse? Would the concept of temporal ordering even exist between multiverses? Presumably not.

But let’s ignore that for a moment and keep the focus on our own universe. We’ve established that it’s difficult to use temporal ordering to learn species rank, but one might wonder if there are other markers we could use to rank species.

In fact, virtually any arbitrary metric could be used to label species. For instance, we might decide to use distance from the sun, in which case we can say that humans, being the only intelligence on Earth[1] get the label of “first.”

But this won’t give us an indexical update. If you think it would, you’re making a mistake known as the "Texas sharpshooter fallacy." The canonical metaphor for the fallacy is a man shooting randomly at his barn, hitting a spot completely at random, and then drawing a target right over where the bullet hit. Then everyone gathers round and thinks to themselves "Wow! What were the chances he would hit that exact target 3.231 feet from the left and 8.654 feet off the ground?"

The lesson for us is that when you condition on a certain event happening (for instance, the bullet hitting some extremely specific spot on the barn, or being closest to the sun), you also need to condition on the process that selected that event. It's not "what is the probability that you would hit a bullseye at coordinate (3.231, 8.654)?" it's "what is the probability that you would hit a bullseye drawn right where the bullet hit?" The answer to the second question is obviously "100%."

In the anthropic case, if every species were to assign a ranking by looking around, finding the closest star/large celestial landmark, and choosing to rank based on that, then they would all rank themselves number 1. Thus, the probability of being rank 1 using this procedure is 100% in all universes, and no update is possible.

Instead, what you would need to do is rank yourself according to some kind of universal anchor that would be identified identically by all species in the universe/multiverse, wherever they are. In a single universe, this could be time since the Big Bang, but that would mostly only effect your prior on the typical number of species within a single universe;[2] if you believed there might be a multiverse you wouldn’t be able to do any serious indexical updating because you wouldn’t know how many other life-bearing universes there were. 

And, as we mentioned, indexing those would be basically impossible. Perhaps you could rank multiverses by “largest gravitational constant” or something similar, but updating would still require you to know how much life existed in each and every multiverse. The point is, without significant global information about the entirety of existence, you’re not going to be able to perform indexical updates about your species. If you’re using the SSA, you’ll have trouble moving beyond your prior for species-level information[3] and if you’re using the SIA, you’ll be locked into a “presumptuous” view of the universe where you’re unduly biased towards a multitude of species.

Now, the fact that you need global information to perform indexical species updates is a practical objection, not a theoretical one. You can’t, as far as I can tell, use this fact as a first principle from which to design an anthropic assumption. But it’s still something to keep in mind when we explore the PPA, since it is only these sorts of fully-anchored species-level updates which can actually cause indexical SSAish updates to your model’s parameters. For all intents and purposes, you will never be able to learn the kind of information that would cause the PPA to perform an unusual update.

The next piece is "The Fermi Paradox, Fine-Tuning, and the SSA"

item.title: PPA 6: Indexical Models Don't Have Diversity Biases
item.description:
[This is the sixth piece in my series on the Parametric Process Assumption (PPA), a new model of anthropics. You should start here if you are just seeing this for the first time.

The previous piece is "Improper Priors and the Infinite SIA."

TLDR:

  • Neither the SSA nor SIA have any bias towards observer attributes which aren't directly correlated with the number of observers in the universe
  • For the Basic Model, which we discuss more at the end of the series, this will apply to any properties of various species (physiology, local universe observations, etc.) which don't a priori tell us something about how long our species will survive.

The next piece is "Temporal Consistency and Texas Sharpshooting."]


Another misconception I had at one point was that the SIA produced a great bias for diversity than the SSA.

By diversity, I mean basically any measure of observers having different experiences from my own. That could mean the existence of a person having a different childhood from mine, or it could mean four-armed green-skinned aliens from the Andromeda Galaxy. Literally anything that isn’t directly correlated with the number of observers in the universe counts.[1]

Both the SIA and SSA update on this type of information identically. To see why, let's start with a simple example where, with 50% probability, only humans exist, and with 50% probability we have a more diverse universe where in addition to the humans we also have an equal number of aliens. Unconditionally, the SIA does say the alien universe is more likely, but once we learn we are human, we revert to the universe prior and the bias disappears:

So, in practice, the conditional SIA is agnostic about observers different from us in ways we can observe, which includes all of our experiences up to this point.

What about the SSA? It is true that if you run the same scenario through the SSA, you will predictably find that conditioning on your humanity makes the aliens less likely to exist:

These examples were what originally convinced me that the SSA had a bias for less diversity, but they're actually focusing on the wrong things entirely.[2] The second universe in this example isn't just more diverse, it's also contains twice as many observers, and we already know that the SIA prefers bigger universes. We could just as easily image a situation where the smaller universe was more diverse, and then it would be the SSA which updates to a bigger universe.

Consider for instance a universe prior where with 50% probability there are 4N humans, and with 50% probability there are N humans and N aliens. Putting both side-by-side (with the SSA on top and the SIA on bottom) it's immediately clear that the SSA puts twice as much relative weight onto the "Human + Alien" universe.

That's because anthropic biases only concern themselves with universe size. If you use a model where size and diversity aren't correlated, then anthropic biases won't play into it.

More broadly, the reason the first "Humans or Humans + Aliens" model is wrong is because it assumes that humans must exist no matter what, and the only real question is what else exists besides. If we don't privilege humans in this way, but rather consider them just one type of life that might have existed among many, then we'll find it a lot easier to construct examples where diversity doesn't matter.

For instance, suppose for the sake of argument we knew that the universe would independently produce exactly two different species, and this meant there were exactly 3 equally likely outcomes:

  • Both were human
  • One was human and one was alien
  • Both were alien

In this case, regardless of whether we used the SSA or the SIA, both the unconditional and conditional distributions would be identical:

This sort of effect is the same we'll see in the Basic Model later in this series. There, the diversity variable will apply at a species-level, referencing any of an observer's various properties (physiology, distance to closest star, etc.) which don't a priori tell them something about how long their species will survive. Thanks to the results above, we will be able to safely ignore those variables in our analysis.

The next piece is "Temporal Consistency in Anthropics"
